861.event_title: Ranjit Singh accepts the Sutlej frontier with the British
861.event: Ranjit Singh, ruler of the Sikh kingdom of Punjab, at first rejected the East India Company's terms and crossed the Sutlej to take territory on its southern bank, and both sides began preparing for war when the British sent a force under David Ochterlony to Ludhiana. He then signed the Treaty of Amritsar, which fixed his frontier broadly along the Sutlej while leaving him free to act north of the river. Britannica notes that the episode gave him great respect for the Company's disciplined troops and a determination never to fight them, and that his later conquests were to the west and north.
861.explanation: A rising ruler chose not to fight a stronger power, and used the security of that frontier to expand where his rivals were weaker.
861.tie_back: The kural advises avoiding enmity with the stronger while not shrinking from contests with the weaker, which is exactly the course Ranjit Singh followed after 1809.
861._accuracy_note: A very close match: the sources document both his decision never to fight the British and his subsequent conquests in other directions.

862.event_title: Maximilian's Mexican empire falls once French troops leave
862.event: Maximilian, an Austrian archduke, became emperor of Mexico in 1864 with the backing of French troops sent by Napoleon III. Under diplomatic pressure from the United States and rising costs at home, Napoleon withdrew the French army, which had fully embarked by March 1867, leaving Maximilian with a small force of foreign volunteers and largely untrained Mexican draftees. Besieged by republican forces at Querétaro, his army surrendered in May 1867, and he was executed in June.
862.explanation: A regime that lacked broad support among its own subjects, lost its only powerful ally and had little strength of its own collapsed within months.
862.tie_back: The kural asks how one without the affection of his people, without strong allies and without strength of his own could ever overcome his enemy, and Maximilian's fall answers it.
862._accuracy_note: All three deficits of the kural are visible in the documented collapse, though the lack of popular support is a historians' assessment rather than a measured fact.

863.event_title: Ethelred the Unready flees to Normandy
863.event: Ethelred II, whose byname Unready meant ill-advised or lacking counsel, failed to keep the loyalty of many of his subjects and tried to protect England from Viking raids by paying the Danes large sums of tribute known as the Danegeld. The payments did not stop the raids, and by 1012 some 48,000 pounds of silver was being paid to Danes camped in London. In 1013 King Sweyn of Denmark invaded, was accepted as king, and Ethelred fled to Normandy.
863.explanation: A king remembered for poor counsel, weak military leadership and the loss of his subjects' allegiance was easily displaced by a determined foe.
863.tie_back: The kural lists fear, lack of understanding, inability to keep others in accord and failure to give as the marks of one who is easy prey, and Ethelred's reign shows several of these at once.
863._accuracy_note: The sources document his poor counsel, lost allegiance and weak defence, but not stinginess, so the fit covers most rather than all of the kural's four faults.

864.event_title: Zinedine Zidane is sent off in the World Cup final
864.event: In extra time of the 2006 FIFA World Cup final between France and Italy, French captain Zinedine Zidane head-butted Italian defender Marco Materazzi in the chest after an exchange of words, and the referee sent him off. The match ended 1-1 and Italy won the penalty shoot-out 5-3, with France's David Trezeguet missing his kick. It was the last match of Zidane's playing career, and FIFA later fined and banned both players.
864.explanation: One of the greatest players of his era ended his career not in defeat by skill but by a moment of uncontrolled anger, removing France's leader before the decisive shoot-out.
864.tie_back: The kural says one whose anger never leaves him and who lacks inner restraint can be overcome by anyone, anywhere, and a single provoked outburst cost Zidane his final match.
864._accuracy_note: A vivid illustration of anger handing the opponent an advantage, though Zidane was not habitually irascible, so it shows the lapse rather than a settled temper.

865.event_title: Honorius refuses terms and Alaric sacks Rome
865.event: The Western Roman emperor Honorius, based in Ravenna, had his leading general Stilicho arrested and executed in 408, after which many soldiers of barbarian origin defected to the Visigothic leader Alaric. Honorius repeatedly refused Alaric's demands during sieges of Rome in 408 and 409. In August 410 Alaric's forces entered Rome, which had not been taken by a foreign enemy for nearly 800 years, and occupied it for three days.
865.explanation: An emperor who removed his ablest defender and would neither fight effectively nor negotiate gave his enemy an opportunity it could hardly have hoped for.
865.tie_back: The kural says one who does not follow the right path, does not do what is fitting and has no care for disgrace is a delight to his enemies, and Honorius's conduct handed Alaric the city.
865._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for failing to do what was fitting; judging Honorius's character and indifference to disgrace is historians' interpretation rather than documented fact.

866.event_title: The Otrar incident provokes Genghis Khan against Khwarezm
866.place: Otrar, Kazakhstan, and Khwarezm, Central Asia
866.event: The governor of the Khwarezmian frontier city of Otrar seized a caravan of Muslim merchants travelling under Genghis Khan's protection and had them killed. The Khwarezm-Shah Ala al-Din Muhammad refused to give satisfaction and ordered the execution of Mongol envoys. Genghis Khan then invaded, and between 1218 and 1220 his armies overran the Khwarezmian empire across what is now Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Iran.
866.explanation: Greed for a caravan's goods and an angry rejection of diplomacy drew a far more dangerous enemy into a war that destroyed the shah's empire.
866.tie_back: The kural says the enmity of one blinded by anger and swollen with desire is welcome to his foes, since he brings about his own defeat, as the shah and his governor did at Otrar.
866._accuracy_note: Both greed and anger are documented in the provocation, though they belong partly to the governor and partly to the shah rather than to one man.

867.event_title: Truman relieves General MacArthur of his commands
867.event: During the Korean War, General Douglas MacArthur publicly called for a wider war, despite a December 1950 directive requiring that statements on military and foreign policy be cleared first. After a letter of his criticising the administration's limited-war policy was read in Congress in April 1951, President Harry Truman relieved him of his commands, stating that MacArthur could not give wholehearted support to the policies of the United States and the United Nations. The public and congressional reaction against Truman was overwhelming, with some calling for his impeachment.
867.explanation: Truman chose open conflict with a celebrated subordinate who kept acting against policy, accepting a heavy political price to restore civilian control.
867.tie_back: The kural says the enmity of one who stays close to you yet acts unworthily should be taken on even at a cost, and Truman paid in popularity to make that break.
867._accuracy_note: Fits the 'close associate acting unworthily' reading well; describing MacArthur's conduct as unworthy reflects the government's view, which the sources document.

868.event_title: Richard II is deserted and deposed
868.event: Richard II's authoritarian rule and reliance on favourites alienated many nobles, and in 1399, on the death of John of Gaunt, he confiscated the vast Lancaster estates that should have passed to his exiled cousin Henry Bolingbroke. While Richard was in Ireland, Henry landed in England, and leading nobles and many others joined him, while many of the soldiers Richard brought back to Wales deserted. Richard surrendered in August and was deposed, and Henry was crowned as Henry IV.
868.explanation: A king who had alienated those around him found, at the moment of need, that almost no one would stand with him.
868.tie_back: The kural says a man of many faults ends up without allies, and that very friendlessness becomes his enemy's strength, as Richard's isolation became Henry's opportunity.
868._accuracy_note: Strong illustration of friendlessness as the enemy's advantage; calling Richard a man 'without virtues' would be unfair, since the sources also note his patronage of the arts.

869.event_title: Frederick the Great routs a divided army at Rossbach
869.event: During the Seven Years' War, Frederick II of Prussia, with about 21,000 men, faced a combined French and Imperial army of at least 41,000 whose commanders, Soubise and Saxe-Hildburghausen, were at odds with each other. As the allied army marched in columns to outflank him, Prussian cavalry under Friedrich Wilhelm von Seydlitz struck from behind cover and the allied force broke. In less than two hours the allies suffered thousands of casualties and many prisoners, while Prussian losses were around 550.
869.explanation: A much smaller but well-led army won one of the most lopsided victories of the century against a larger force hampered by divided and poorly judged command.
869.tie_back: The kural says those who fight will never lack joy if their enemies lack understanding, and Rossbach shows how an opponent's poor judgment hands victory to the attacker.
869._accuracy_note: Fits the 'unwise enemy' half of the kural; the sources document divided command and a rout but do not establish fearfulness, so the fit is partial.

870.event_title: Howe halts after Long Island and Washington's army escapes
870.event: After defeating the inexperienced Continental Army at the Battle of Long Island on 27 August 1776, British General William Howe halted his attack and began siege works rather than pressing the assault, overruling subordinates who argued for a renewed attack. On the night of 29-30 August, George Washington ferried about 9,000 troops across the East River to Manhattan, helped at dawn by fog. Howe did not pursue, and the American army survived to fight on.
870.explanation: A commander who held every advantage over a raw, untrained army let the chance of a decisive victory slip away.
870.tie_back: The kural says one who will not take even the easy gain of opposing an untrained foe will never win glory, and Howe's pause at Brooklyn is remembered as just such a missed opportunity.
870._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit; Howe's reasons are debated, and later criticism of him rather than a documented loss of glory is what links the event to the kural.
